summary: Describes how to map Group 3 fax capability identification bits from ITU T.30 into the Internet fax feature schema. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Old fax machines announce abilities with special signals. This translates those signals into the newer written description used for Internet fax.

questions: how to map t.30 bits to internet fax features
what is a feature set expression
subtitle: How the capability bits of a Group 3 fax machine translate into the feature expressions used by Internet fax.

tldr.problem: A Group 3 fax machine announces what it can receive with bits in ITU T.30 DIS/DTC frames, but Internet fax systems describe capabilities with media feature tags and feature set expressions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo surveys the media-related T.30 bits, lays out their dependencies as decision tables, and gives for each table row a feature set expression, plus a procedure to combine the pieces and to reverse the mapping.
tldr.outcome: An implementer can turn any T.30 capability mask into an Internet fax capability statement, with two worked examples. It is an Informational memo and says it introduces no new security concerns.

today: RFC 2880 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion to the fax feature schema in RFC 2879, and it says it introduces no additional security concerns beyond those discussed there.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2880 describes how to map Group 3 fax capability identification bits, defined in ITU T.30, into the Internet fax feature schema of RFC 2879. It is a companion to that schema document, which profiles the media feature registration mechanisms for capability identification between extended Internet fax systems (called eifax systems).

The memo is organized in steps: how feature tags combine (section 2), a survey of the relevant T.30 bits (section 3), the dependencies between those bits as decision tables (section 4), the formal mapping (section 5), and examples (section 6). Discussion was to take place on the Internet fax mailing list.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of fax machines describe themselves in different languages. This memo is the translator between them.

sections.title: Feature Tags, Collections and Sets
sections.content:
A fax document can be described by media features. A feature tag with its value is one component of a feature collection, which describes one instance of a document, such as a printed fax. A feature set holds a number of collections, so it can describe several treatments of one document, several documents under one treatment, or a mix.

A feature set is written with predicates: functions that yield TRUE when a feature collection describes an acceptable fax document instance and FALSE otherwise. The memo uses (| p1 p2 ... pn) for logical OR and (& p1 p2 ... pn) for logical AND. A feature set can therefore describe either the rendering needs of a document or the capabilities of a receiving eifax system.

The RFC compares these to T.30 frames: a feature tag is like a single bit in a DCS frame, a feature collection corresponds to a whole DCS frame, and a feature set corresponds to a DIS or DTC frame. In T.30 the dependencies between capabilities are implicit; in the feature set framework they are explicit.
sections.eli5: A tag is one fact, like "this page is black and white". A collection is a full description of one page. A set is a list of all the kinds of pages a machine will accept.

sections.title: The Media-Related T.30 Bits
sections.content:
Section 3 walks through the DIS/DTC bits that relate to media handling; bits not mentioned are considered unrelated to media features. Many describe an optional extra on top of a mandatory baseline. Every Group 3 fax system must support a basic resolution of 200*100dpi (8*3.85dpmm), Modified Huffman (MH) one-dimensional coding for bi-level images, a 215mm paper width, a 297mm paper length and A4 paper size.

Setting a bit adds to that baseline. For example, bit 15 adds 200*200dpi, bit 16 adds Modified Read (MR) two-dimensional coding, bit 31 adds Modified Modified Read (MMR), bit 68 adds JPEG coding of multi-level images, bit 69 adds colour in addition to grey-scale, and bits 76 and 77 add North American letter and legal paper. Bits 17 to 20 allow wider (255mm, 303mm) and longer (364mm, unlimited) pages.

Several bits have side effects worth noting. JBIG for bi-level images uses 128 lines per stripe unless bit 79 allows other stripe sizes, and standard MRC support uses a maximum stripe size of 256 lines until bit 95 raises it to a full page. Bits 44 and 45 give the preferred units (inch or metric); the two measures differ slightly, but terminals must accept either and distort the image if needed.
sections.eli5: Every fax machine must handle a plain black-and-white page of a standard size. Extra switches say "I can also do sharper pictures, bigger paper or colour".

sections.title: Dependencies Between T.30 Bits
sections.content:
Section 4 states which combinations of DIS/DTC bits are allowed, using decision tables. In a table, 0 and 1 are bit values, x means either value, an asterisk before a value (star-zero or star-one) means the bit must have that value or the combination is invalid, and a hash sign marks bits combined into a number.

The tables cover four areas: image coding (bi-level, multi-level and MRC format), resolution and units, colour capabilities, and document size. For instance, multi-level coding such as JPEG requires bit 15 (200*200dpi) to be set, and MRC mode is a number from 1 to 7 taken from bits 92, 93 and 94, where all zeros means MRC is not accepted. Some combinations are marked invalid, such as setting both bits 17 and 18, which is interpreted as bit 17 clear and bit 18 set.
sections.eli5: Some switches only make sense together, like needing a bigger backpack before packing a bigger book. The tables list which combinations are allowed.

sections.title: Building the Feature Set Expression
sections.content:
Section 5 restates each decision table with a feature set expression in place of the description. To convert a DIS frame, match its bits against each table; exactly one row of each table or sub-table matches, and its expression is collected. Sub-tables in the resolution table are joined with OR, sub-tables in the colour and size tables with AND, and the tables are finally combined as (& (| T511 T512 ) T513 T52 T53 T54 ).

The expressions use tags such as color, image-coding, dpi, dpi-xyratio, MRC-mode and Paper-size. Resolutions are written as integers or ratios, so 200*100dpi becomes (dpi=200) with (dpi-xyratio=200/100), and the metric equivalents are given in dpi (for example 204 for 8dpmm).

The reverse direction uses the matching algorithm of RFC 2533: OR together the bit masks of every row whose expression is completely contained by the given feature set, using 0 wherever a table shows x. The RFC warns that the result may need other capabilities that DIS bits do not express, such as the TIFF file structure.
sections.eli5: To translate, you look up each group of switches in a table, copy down the matching phrase, and glue the phrases together with AND and OR.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first example is a common black-and-white fax machine with bits 15, 16, 31, 42 and 76 set. The tables yield (color=binary), (image-coding=[MH,MR,MMR]), (MRC-mode=0), a set of resolution options including 300*300dpi, (size-x<=2150/254) and (Paper-size=[A4,Letter]). Section 6.1.1 then adds a TIFF file structure capability to show how an Internet fax device would extend the T.30-derived result.

The second example is a full-featured colour fax machine with JPEG, full colour, no subsampling, MRC mode 1 and the extra multi-level resolutions. Its simplified result has three alternatives: binary, grey and full colour, each with its own coding, resolution and colour-space constraints (for example (color-space=CIELAB)).

The RFC stresses that the algorithms build capability expressions that might be incorporated into eifax statements; they do not by themselves create equivalent Internet fax capability statements.
sections.eli5: The memo shows two real-looking machines, a plain black-and-white one and a fancy colour one, and translates each one's switches step by step.
